In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of chromosomal abnormalities in acute lymphoblast leukemia.

the identification of the genetic changes in the cells of patients with leukemia and the relationship of these genetic changes to the clinical features of the leukemia and to the response of the leukemia to treatment.
the identification of chromosomal abnormalities and the elucidation of their biological and clinical significance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of a chromosomal abnormality in ALL is of importance, and its recognition is essential in order to identify the patient with a high risk of relapse and for whom alternative therapeutic approaches should be considered.
the prognostic significance of chromosomal abnormalities in ALL is complex, and that the prognostically important chromosomal abnormalities are not yet known.

the prognosis in ALL depends on the presence or absence of the following factors: the patient's age, the leukemic blast cell phenotype, the number and ploidy of chromosomes, the presence of a translocation, and the presence of a hyperdiploid clone with a modal number of chromosomes greater than 50.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cytogenetic findings are important in ALL, but their role is changing as we learn more about the molecular mechanisms of leukemogenic change and as alternative treatment strategies are developed for patients who are at high-risk because of their chromosome findings.
the prognostic importance and clinical utility of chromosome findings in childhood ALL are increasing.

the chromosomal findings in ALL can be divided into three categories: 1) structural changes that are associated with particular blast cell features and are associated with a favorable or an unfavorable prognosis, 2) translocations involving the oncogenes of the immunoglobulin or the T-cell receptor loci, and 3) other translocations, some of which are associated with a particular blast cell phenotype and a favorable prognosis, and others with an unfavorable prognosis and a high frequency of relapse.
The main takeaway from our work is that

chromosomal abnormalities can have prognostic value, but the value of chromosomal findings is not absolute, and other factors, including age, immunophenotype, and response to therapy, are equally or more important.
the presence or absence of a chromosomal abnormality in a patient with ALL is a powerful prognostic factor and should be incorporated into risk group assignments.
cytogenetic analysis remains an important prognostic factor in childhood ALL and that patients with certain cytogenetic abnormalities may benefit from alternative therapy.
